script.title: What to do with your tax refund: a plan with real numbers
script.hook: $2,800 refund. Here's exactly where every dollar goes, step by step.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Twenty-eight hundred dollars. That's our example refund today, and by the end of this video every dollar will have a job. The average refund is a big chunk of money for most people early in their career, and it usually disappears within a few weeks without a plan. We'll go step by step, with real numbers, and you can swap in your own.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes holding a large envelope at a whiteboard. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The example
segments.narration: Our example: a fictional person earning fifty thousand a year, with three hundred in savings, twenty-two hundred on a credit card at twenty-four percent, and a car that needs new tyres soon. The refund is twenty-eight hundred dollars. Fictional, but very typical.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a profile card with three small icons. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1
segments.narration: Step one: the buffer. With only three hundred saved, any surprise goes on the card. So the first seven hundred goes to savings, taking it to a thousand. Keep it in an insured high-yield savings account, separate from checking.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a jar filling to a line. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2
segments.narration: Step two: the highest-interest debt. The card charges twenty-four percent, roughly forty-four dollars a month in interest on this balance. Fifteen hundred goes to the card. That cuts the interest by about thirty dollars a month straight away.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a card shrinking. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3
segments.narration: Step three: the known cost. Tyres are coming, about four hundred dollars. That's not an emergency, it's a bill you can see. Three hundred goes into a car sinking fund now, and the rest builds from your regular budget.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small jar with a tyre. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4
segments.narration: Step four: the treat. Three hundred dollars, about ten percent, for something you'll enjoy. This is part of the plan, not a failure of it. Plans with nothing fun in them get abandoned.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small gift box. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The split
segments.narration: So: seven hundred to savings, fifteen hundred to the card, three hundred to the car fund, three hundred for fun. Twenty-eight hundred, all assigned. Use Form 8888 when you file to split it automatically, or move it the day it lands.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. four jars in a row. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If no debt
segments.narration: If you don't have high-interest debt, step two changes. Many people put that money into a Roth or Traditional IRA instead, and before April fifteenth you can often choose to count it for last year. Remember that investing involves risk, including loss of principal.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a sprout in a pot. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Next year
segments.narration: Finally, look at why the refund was this size. A twenty-eight hundred refund is about two hundred and thirty dollars a month that came out of your paychecks. If you'd rather have that monthly, run the IRS withholding estimator and update your W-4.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a paycheck with a slider. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.narration: Recap: buffer first, then the highest-rate debt, then the costs you can see coming, and one planned treat. Decide it before the money lands. Examples are hypothetical and for education only. Not financial or tax advice.

script.title: Your W-4, explained: stop overpaying (or owing) every April
script.hook: 4 W-4 myths that cost you money, from a $3,000 refund to a surprise bill.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Four W-4 myths, and every one of them costs real money. Maybe you get a three thousand dollar refund every year, which is two hundred and fifty dollars a month that left your paychecks and came back late, with no interest. Or maybe you owe every April. Both come down to one form. Let's check the myths against the facts.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes holding a form with a magnifying glass. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Myth 1
segments.narration: Myth one: a big refund means you did taxes well. Fact: a refund means too much was withheld. Your employer takes an estimate of your tax out of each paycheck. Withheld too much, you get it back. Too little, you owe. The W-4 is the dial.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a dial with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Myth 2
segments.narration: Myth two: you claim allowances, zero or one. Fact: the current W-4 doesn't use allowances. It has steps instead. Step one is your filing status, which sets the starting point. Step three is credits for children and other dependents, which make paychecks bigger.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a crossed-out old form next to a new one. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Myth 3
segments.narration: Myth three: two jobs sort themselves out. Fact: each employer withholds as if it's your only job, so two jobs, or two working spouses, usually means owing. That's what step two is for. Skip it when it applies and April gets expensive.
segments.on_screen_text: Myth: two jobs work themselves out
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two briefcases with a warning sign. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Myth 4
segments.narration: Myth four: you only touch the W-4 when you start a job. Fact: you can change it any time. Check it after a new job, a second job, marriage, a baby, a big raise, and once in spring when last year's numbers are fresh.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar with several circled dates. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Real numbers: refund
segments.narration: Now the real numbers. You got a three thousand dollar refund and want it closer to zero. Run the free IRS Tax Withholding Estimator. If it says you're over-withholding by about that much, it will suggest entries that shrink it, roughly a hundred and fifteen dollars more per biweekly paycheck.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calculator next to a paycheck. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Real numbers: owing
segments.narration: Owe instead? Do the opposite. Owed nine hundred? Step four c, extra withholding per paycheck, is the simplest dial: about thirty-five dollars per biweekly paycheck covers it.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a slider moving up. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: a refund means you overpaid, owing means you underpaid, there are no allowances any more, two jobs need step two, and you can change it any time. Use the IRS estimator, change only what it suggests, and check again next spring. Educational, not tax advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the mascot holding a balanced dial. No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: Where's my tax refund? How refunds work, and what slows them down
script.hook: Most refunds arrive in 21 days. Here's why yours might not.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Most e-filed tax returns with direct deposit get their refund within twenty-one days. If yours hasn't arrived, there's usually a reason, and usually it's fixable. Here's how refund processing works, and what slows it down.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes next to a calendar with three weeks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How it works
segments.narration: When you e-file, the IRS first accepts the return, then processes it, checks it against forms like your W-2s and 1099s, approves the refund and sends it. Where's My Refund shows those stages: received, approved, sent.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a conveyor belt with three stops. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Paper
segments.narration: Paper returns go through the same steps by hand, and that can add weeks. E-file with direct deposit is the fastest combination.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a snail carrying an envelope. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The legal hold
segments.narration: If you claim the Earned Income Tax Credit or the Additional Child Tax Credit, the law requires the IRS to wait until mid-February before issuing those refunds, to catch fraud. Many of those refunds then arrive by early March.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a gate opening in mid-February. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Identity checks
segments.narration: Sometimes the IRS needs to confirm it's really you before releasing the refund. You'll get a letter in the post with instructions. Respond quickly, using IRS dot gov or the number on the letter, which you can verify on IRS dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. an envelope with a badge. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Errors
segments.narration: Errors slow things down too: a missing 1099, a math mistake, or a bank account number with one wrong digit. If the deposit bounces, the refund usually comes as a paper check instead.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a form with one line circled. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Offsets
segments.narration: And sometimes part of the refund is used to pay other debts, like past-due child support, some federal debts, or state taxes. You'll get a notice if that happens.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. coins diverted to another jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: When to call
segments.narration: Calling the IRS usually only helps if it's been more than twenty-one days since you e-filed, six weeks since you mailed a paper return, or the tool tells you to call.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a phone with a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Scams
segments.narration: While you wait, watch for scams. The IRS starts contact by mail, not texts or emails. Never click a refund link. Check your status yourself on IRS dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a phone with a stop sign. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: e-file with direct deposit, expect up to about twenty-one days, longer for early filers claiming EITC or ACTC, respond quickly to any letter, and check once a day. Educational, not tax advice. Check IRS dot gov for your situation.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a sticky note with three ticks. No text, no logos, no real people.
